Unified Results, Analysis and Supporting Evidence

A single narrative and evidence chain for marginal price formation in the GB Balancing Mechanism, resolving the analysis from active-side technology regimes to BMU identity and battery displacement.

Study window: 1 January 2023–31 December 2025 · Generated 17 July 2026, 12:06 GMT Daylight Time · Source narrative: Combined RQs + evidence D2.docx
50,684valid Settlement Periods
26,987bid-active / long-system SPs
23,697offer-active / short-system SPs
12integrated main-text figures

Introduction –

This study makes three principal empirical contributions. First, it reconstructs marginal price formation separately for long-system bid-active and short-system offer-active periods, demonstrating that pooled technology statistics conceal distinct participant and price regimes. Second, it resolves attributed marginality from technology to plant-family and BMU level, showing that repeated marginality, conditional price distributions and model attribution are concentrated but analytically distinct. Third, it traces the emergence of battery storage as a major marginal participant, demonstrating that its aggregate role is dispersed across the fleet, stronger in long-system price formation and increasingly favourable relative to the immediate non-battery alternatives in the observed balancing ladder.

Contribution 1: the BM contains two distinct side-conditioned price-forming regimes

Weighting convention.

Unless stated otherwise, marginal shares allocate one unit of weight per Settlement Period across any co-marginal BMUs. Chapter 3 defines this convention formally; the main figures therefore use the simpler term share of attributed marginality.

  • The analysis begins by separating the Balancing Mechanism into the economically relevant stack for each system condition.
  • Positive NIV identifies a short system in which the offer stack is active; negative NIV identifies a long system in which the bid stack is active.
  • Of 50,684 valid Settlement Periods, 26,987 were bid-active and 23,697 were offer-active.
  • This split is substantive rather than merely methodological: the two regimes differ in participant composition and in the level, shape and sign of the System Price distributions associated with marginal identity.
  • The principal descriptive measure is therefore the share of attributed marginality within each active side. Each Settlement Period contributes a total weight of one across its co-marginal BMUs, preserving all tied identities without allowing heavily tied periods to dominate the descriptive results.
Figure 1. Technology composition by active side

Figure 1. Technology composition of attributed marginality in bid-active and offer-active Settlement Periods.

Full analytical report CSV file

Main-text figure. Establishes the shared CCGT–battery core and the asymmetry of the surrounding fleets.

  • CCGT remained the leading marginal technology in both regimes, accounting for approximately 44% of bid-active and 46% of offer-active attributed marginality.
  • Battery storage was unusually balanced across the two regimes at about 17% on each side.
  • Beyond this common core, however, the technology mix diverged sharply.
  • Pumped storage was strongly offer-oriented, whereas wind and biomass were concentrated on the bid side.
  • The GB BM should therefore not be represented by a single pooled technology ranking: the same leading technologies operate within materially different surrounding fleets
Figure 2. Published System Price conditional on marginal technology

Figure 2. Side-conditioned System Price distributions associated with each attributed marginal technology.

Full analytical report CSV file

Main-text figure. Separates marginal frequency from the price distributions associated with each attributed technology.

  • The conditional price distributions show that greater marginal frequency should not be equated with a single technology-specific price effect.
  • In offer-active periods, the central distributions of battery, CCGT and pumped storage overlap substantially, while CCGT and pumped storage extend further into high-price outcomes.
  • On the bid side, the principal dispatchable technologies again occupy broadly similar central ranges, but wind is structurally distinct, with a median close to zero and a deeply negative lower tail.
  • The sharper technological differences therefore lie in the directional tails rather than in uniformly separated central prices.
  • These distributions remain descriptive. Marginal technology identity is associated with the conditions under which each technology appears; the figure does not estimate causal technology effects on System Price.
Figure 3. Evolution of marginal technology shares, 2023–2025

Figure 3. Quarterly evolution of attributed marginality by active side.

Full analytical report CSV file

Main-text figure. Provides the temporal answer to RQ1 and establishes the growth of battery marginality used later in the battery synthesis.

  • Battery marginality expanded in both regimes, with the stronger transition during bid-active, long-system periods.
  • Its bid-side share rose from 1% in 2023 Q1 to 36% in 2025 Q4, while CCGT fell from 55% to 34%; battery exceeded CCGT in the final two quarters of 2025.
  • On the offer side, battery increased from 3% to 27%, coinciding with a decline in pumped storage from 33% to 10%, while CCGT remained the leading technology and ended at 45%.
  • The evidence supports a shift in market composition rather than a causal displacement claim.
  • Battery fleet capacity and the number of active battery BMUs also expanded substantially over the period, so the trajectory demonstrates growing participation at the margin but does not isolate behavioural change per BMU or per GW.
Figure 4. Technology composition across NIV intensity

Figure 4. Technology composition and System Price across the direction and intensity of NIV.

Full analytical report CSV file

Main-text figure. Shows that system condition affects marginal identity continuously, not only through the sign of NIV.

  • The composition of attributed marginality changes with the severity as well as the direction of imbalance.
  • Wind dominates the most strongly long conditions, accounting for 52% of marginal weight in the outer long-system bin, while CCGT becomes increasingly prominent as the system approaches balance.
  • Immediately either side of zero, CCGT has the same 49% share but the median System Price differs markedly, reinforcing that bid-active and offer-active periods form distinct economic regimes rather than a continuous pooled distribution.
  • Within short-system conditions, battery participation rises as positive NIV becomes larger, although the sparsely populated outer bins should carry less evidential weight.
  • The principal conclusion is that technology composition varies systematically across the imbalance distribution: wind is concentrated in deep surplus, CCGT is strongest near balance, and battery and other flexible technologies become more prominent as the system moves into shortness

Main contribution

  • Marginal price formation remained anchored by CCGT but became more technologically diverse between 2023 and 2025. The transition was most pronounced on the bid side, where battery storage became a leading marginal technology.
  • The active-side split is the organising result: long-system bid and short-system offer periods share a CCGT–battery core but differ in their surrounding fleets, associated price distributions and temporal trajectories.

Contribution 2: BMU-level analysis reveals concentration and heterogeneity concealed by fuel type

  • The second contribution changes the unit of analysis from technology to the individual Balancing Mechanism Unit.
  • It separates three related but distinct objects: how often a BMU is attributed as marginal, how strongly its identity contributes to variation in the fitted model overall, and whether its active appearances are associated with predictions above or below the model baseline.
  • Repeated marginality is measured using Settlement Period-weighted marginal share, global attribution using global mean absolute SHAP, and direction using conditional signed SHAP when the feature is active.
Figure 5. Repeated marginality among leading BMUs

Figure 5. Repeated marginality among leading BMUs, expressed as each unit's share of attributed marginality.

Full analytical report CSV file

Main-text figure. Shows concentrated repeated marginality and the absence of individually dominant battery BMUs.

  • The leading 25 BMUs account for 35.6% of total attributed marginality despite representing only 3.2% of the 771 BMUs identified at the margin.
  • The group contains 18 CCGTs, five pumped-storage BMUs and two biomass BMUs, but no batteries. T_HUMR-1 is the leading unit at 2.76% of total marginal weight, while E_DOLLB-1 is the highest-ranked battery at 32nd and accounts for 0.75%.
  • Battery’s substantial technology-level role therefore does not arise from a small group of repeatedly dominant assets.
  • It is distributed across a comparatively atomised fleet.
  • This is a fragmentation result, not evidence that individual batteries are economically irrelevant.
  • The side split also reveals substantial heterogeneity within technologies: some CCGTs are predominantly marginal during long-system periods, while others are concentrated on the offer side.
Appendix Figure A5. Battery co-marginality by year and active side

Appendix Figure A5. Incidence and technology composition of battery co-marginality by year and active side.

Full analytical report CSV file

Appendix figure. Panel A reports how often battery-marginal Settlement Periods contain a co-marginal set; Panel B shows the technology composition of those tied sets.

  • Panel A shows that battery marginality became less frequently co-marginal by 2025.
  • On the bid side, the share of battery-marginal Settlement Periods containing a co-marginal set moved from 25.0% in 2023 to 27.9% in 2024 and 14.4% in 2025; on the offer side, it declined from 30.2% to 21.1% and 10.5%.
  • Battery marginality therefore became more commonly associated with a single marginal candidate, particularly during short-system, offer-active periods.
  • Conditional on co-marginality occurring, however, the tied sets remained strongly battery-clustered. Across every year and active side, at least 74% contained multiple battery BMUs.
  • In 2025, 86.9% of bid-side and 77.1% of offer-side battery co-marginal sets contained multiple batteries; battery-only sets accounted for 78.4% and 69.0%, respectively.
  • The result complements the fragmentation finding: battery marginality is distributed across many individually small BMUs, yet several battery actions often share the same marginal price when a tie occurs.
  • This pattern is consistent with common market signals and possible intra-fleet competition, but it does not establish coordinated bidding or realised revenue cannibalisation. Because Panel B conditions on a shrinking subset, the final figure should report the Settlement Period count underlying each bar.
Figure 6. Global importance and directional association across identity resolution

Figure 6. Global mean absolute SHAP and conditional signed SHAP across technology, plant-family and BMU resolution.

Full analytical report CSV file

Main-text figure. Uses global mean absolute SHAP to select features and signed SHAP to interpret the direction of the same identities.

  • At technology resolution, CCGT offer is the leading global feature, followed by wind bid, pumped-storage offer and CCGT bid.
  • Battery bid and battery offer rank fifth and sixth, confirming that battery identity is materially represented in the technology-level model.
  • Their directional associations are asymmetric: battery bid is associated with lower predicted System Prices, whereas battery offer is associated with higher predictions.
  • At finer resolution, these broad associations resolve into identifiable plant families and BMUs.
  • Battery prominence does not translate into a similarly dominant set of individual assets: only one battery family enters the full plant-family coverage set and no battery BMU enters the corresponding BMU set.
  • The aggregate battery signal therefore fragments across the fleet rather than disappearing economically.
  • Conditional signed SHAP values are model associations rather than causal effects. The technology, plant-family and BMU models are estimated separately, so absolute SHAP magnitudes should be interpreted within each resolution rather than compared mechanically across rows.
Figure 7. Within-technology variation in BMU-level System Price distributions

Figure 7. Within-technology variation in recurrent BMUs' side-conditioned System Price distributions.

Full analytical report CSV file

Main-text figure. Directly demonstrates what a technology median conceals about recurrent BMUs.

  • BMUs within the same technology retain distinct side-conditioned price distributions.
  • On the bid side, leading CCGT medians are relatively compressed, but their lower tails and interquartile ranges differ.
  • On the offer side, differentiation within CCGT is stronger: recurrent units occupy materially different central ranges and upper-tail positions around the common technology benchmark.
  • Pumped-storage BMUs also differ from one another, while the highest-frequency battery BMU does not reproduce the most extreme offer-side signatures.
  • The figure strengthens the unit-level argument by separating both active side and distributional shape.
  • Fuel-type medians conceal recurrent differences in central price, dispersion and directional tails, even though the descriptive evidence does not establish that BMU identity causes those outcomes.
Figure 8. Repeated marginality versus global BMU attribution

Figure 8. Repeated marginality compared with global BMU SHAP attribution.

Full analytical report CSV file

Main-text figure. Shows that frequency and model distinctiveness are positively related but not equivalent.

  • Repeated marginality is positively associated with global BMU attribution, but frequency alone does not determine which identities are most distinctive to the fitted model.
  • Some BMUs combine frequent marginality with strong attribution, while other comparatively frequent units carry much lower attribution in the same role. Conversely, several less frequent offer-side BMUs are associated with large deviations from the model baseline.
  • Battery BMUs remain outside the upper-frequency and upper-attribution region on both sides despite battery’s technology-level importance. This reinforces the conclusion that battery participation and model attribution are dispersed across a broader fleet rather than concentrated among individually dominant units.

Main contribution

  • Fuel-type analysis captures the broad technological direction of marginal price formation, but it cannot identify which units repeatedly reach the margin or show how strongly units within the same technology differ in side, price distribution and model association.
  • Repeated marginality, conditional price level and global attribution are related but distinct. The leading identities are side-specific, and battery’s aggregate prominence is fragmented across many BMUs.

Contribution 3: battery storage became routine, fleet-dispersed and economically asymmetric

  • The preceding sections already establish two parts of the battery result.
  • First, battery storage moved from a peripheral position in 2023 to a major source of attributed marginality by 2025, with the strongest growth during long-system, bid-active periods.
  • Second, this aggregate role was spread across a comparatively fragmented fleet rather than concentrated among a few individually dominant BMUs.
  • The final battery section should therefore not repeat those trajectories. It should ask the narrower remaining question: what kind of price formation did growing battery participation represent, and what immediate non-battery alternatives sat behind battery actions in the observed ladder?

Directional price-tail evidence

  • Battery’s share of all marginal periods on the relevant side can be compared with its share of that side’s extreme-price tail.
  • A lower tail share means that battery is less prevalent in the extreme tail than in marginality generally
Figure 9. Battery marginal participation overall and in directional price tails

Figure 9. Battery's overall marginal share paired with its share in the bid-side P5 and offer-side P95 System Price tails.

Full analytical report CSV file

  • During long-system periods, battery’s share of the bid-side P5 tail rose from 0.7% in 2023 to 19.7% in 2025, alongside an increase in its overall bid-side marginal share from 4.3% to 30.5%.
  • Batteries remained less prevalent in the lowest-price periods than in bid-side marginality generally, but their presence in the lower tail strengthened consistently.
  • This supports a growing role in deep-surplus balancing without claiming dominance of the most negative prices.
  • During short-system periods, battery’s share of the offer-side P95 tail increased from 3.5% to 15.7%, but its overall offer-side marginal share rose more rapidly, from 6.4% to 27.9%.
  • Battery nearly matched its general marginal share in the 2024 upper tail, but this convergence was not sustained in 2025.
  • CCGT and pumped storage therefore retained a stronger position in the highest-priced short-system outcomes.

Fixed-ladder consequence of battery removal: displacement analysis

  • For each battery-marginal observation, the removed battery volume is refilled using the next eligible non-battery actions in the observed ladder.
  • The comparison holds the eligible action ladder fixed; it is not a full no-battery redispatch, an official System Price reconstruction or a consumer-savings estimate.
  • The accepted-action VWAP comparison is favourable to the battery action in every year and widens markedly by 2025.
  • On the offer side, the gap rises from approximately £2/MWh in 2023-2024 to £10.23/MWh in 2025.
  • On the bid side, it reaches £10.24/MWh in 2025.
  • The share of observations in which the battery action is favourable also rises to approximately nine in ten on both sides. The result is therefore not driven solely by a small number of extreme observations.
  • This is a clearer economic contribution than a binary price-maker/price-taker label.
  • Batteries can respond to expected prices when submitting actions and still form the operational margin when accepted.
  • By 2025, their actions commonly sat ahead of less favourable non-battery alternatives in the fixed observed ladder, even though the analysis does not identify market power or a causal effect on the published System Price.

The final replacement margin was heterogeneous

  • The final non-battery BMU reached after the removed battery volume was refilled came from a broad set of assets.
Figure 12. Technology composition at the fixed-ladder replacement margin

Figure 12. Technology of the final non-battery BMU reached after refilling the removed battery volume.

Full analytical report CSV file

  • CCGT formed the largest single technology group, but the most frequently reached individual unit was a load-response asset, and pumped storage, diesel, gas, wind and additional demand-side resources also appeared.
  • The result does not support a simple narrative in which batteries displaced one generic thermal technology or only one segment of the merit order.

Discussion implication: from inter-technology substitution to intra-battery competition

  • The fixed-stack counterfactual and the co-marginality analysis identify two distinct channels of battery influence.
  • The replacement exercise captures inter-technology substitution by identifying the non-battery alternatives behind observed battery actions in the side-specific accepted-action stack.
  • The co-marginality analysis instead shows that, although battery-marginal periods became less frequently tied by 2025, the ties that remained were usually concentrated among multiple battery BMUs.
  • As the fleet expands, this price clustering could shift competition from batteries sitting ahead of conventional alternatives towards batteries competing directly with one another for the same balancing opportunities.
  • This provides a plausible mechanism for future cannibalisation through lower accepted volumes, narrower spreads or reduced revenues per asset, but the present evidence does not show that cannibalisation has already occurred.
  • Testing that mechanism would require evidence on accepted volume, action-price spreads or revenue per active BMU or per MW as battery penetration increases.

Main contribution

  • Battery storage became a genuine and increasingly frequent price-forming participant in the operational sense of reaching the attributed margin. Its role was nevertheless asymmetric across system conditions.
  • Its participation moved progressively toward the long-system bid-side lower tail, while its rapid offer-side growth did not translate into sustained representation among the highest-priced short-system periods.
  • The fixed-ladder evidence shows that this routine role remained economically consequential: by 2025, battery actions were usually more favourable than the non-battery actions required to replace their accepted volume in the observed ladder

Synthesis against the research questions

RQ1: evolution of marginal price formation

  • Marginal price formation in the GB Balancing Mechanism remained anchored by CCGT between 2023 and 2025, but became more technologically diverse and strongly conditioned by system state.
  • Long-system bid and short-system offer periods shared a CCGT–battery core but mobilised different surrounding fleets and were associated with distinct System Price distributions.
  • Battery marginality expanded rapidly on both sides and exceeded CCGT during bid-active periods in late 2025, while CCGT remained dominant on the offer side.
  • Technology composition also varied with NIV intensity, from wind-led marginality under severe long-system conditions to greater CCGT and flexible-technology participation nearer balance and during shortness.

RQ2: what BMU-level analysis adds

  • BMU-level analysis shows that repeated marginality, conditional price distribution and model attribution are related but distinct dimensions of price formation.
  • Repeated marginality is concentrated among a relatively small set of CCGT, pumped-storage and biomass BMUs, but battery marginality is distributed across a broader fleet.
  • Broad technology associations resolve into specific plant families and units, and BMUs within the same technology retain different active-side roles, central prices, dispersion and directional tails.
  • Fuel-type analysis therefore captures the broad technological direction of price formation but cannot show which units repeatedly reach the margin or how strongly individual BMUs differ in price and predictive association.
  • Battery marginality became more often individually resolved by 2025, but the remaining co-marginal sets were predominantly clustered among multiple battery BMUs.

RQ3: battery storage as a price-forming participant

  • Battery storage became a frequent price-forming participant in the operational sense used by this study, with the strongest increase during long-system bid-active periods.
  • Its role was fleet-dispersed rather than concentrated among individually dominant BMUs and remained asymmetric across the price distribution.
  • Battery participation moved steadily toward the lowest bid-side prices, but its rapid growth on the offer side did not produce sustained representation among the highest-priced short-system periods.
  • By 2025, battery actions also commonly sat ahead of less favourable non-battery alternatives in the fixed observed ladder.
  • The concentration of remaining ties within the battery fleet is consistent with a possible future intra-battery competition and cannibalisation mechanism, but it does not demonstrate realised revenue compression.
  • Batteries therefore became routine and economically consequential marginal participants without becoming proportionate setters of the offer-side upper price tail.
